title: An-Nafi', the Benefactor
hookLine: the Benefactor, source of every benefit
tomorrow: a lamp, a glass, a star. what is the light in that verse?

lines: A RIDE. A READ. AN INTRODUCTION.
NOT THE END OF THE LIST.
cards: A ride to an interview. A few minutes reading over someone's application. An introduction to the one person who knows how things work.

Small things for the giver that can change a whole season for the one who gets them. Yesterday's question: Eli wants into a weekend art class, and the application asks for a portfolio and a reference.
What can Amira actually give? She's a student. She can't sign anything official.
Today's Name says that isn't the end of the list.

teach.b: An-Nafi', the Benefactor, source of every benefit. It's the partner of yesterday's Name: harm and help, both in one hand. And in the Qur'an, benefit has a picture.
In Surah ar-Ra'd, the chapter of thunder, rain comes down and the valleys run with it, and foam rises on top, loud and white.
The foam passes away on the banks.

teach.h: OF USE TO MANKIND, IT REMAINETH.
teach.b: Then, in Pickthall's words: "as for that which is of use to mankind, it remaineth in the earth." Here's the line to tell a friend tonight.
In that parable, the foam is what you notice, and the water is what lasts. Usefulness stays. And notice the word: mankind.
Benefit in this verse is for people, all of them. There's also a saying reported from the Prophet, peace be upon him, that the people most beloved to God are the ones most useful to other people.
So what can a student give? Help choosing the best pages. A question to her art teacher about who could write the reference.
A wall in her dad's shop where the drawings can hang. None of it is official. All of it is water, not foam.

how: Muslims count everyday usefulness as charity: the Prophet called removing something harmful from a road an act of sadaqah.

o: the Healer, who cures every sickness
the Provider of each day's food
the Benefactor, source of all benefit

games.q: foam and water — tap the pairs.
p: what is of use to mankind

s: in the parable of the rain, the foam is what lasts
the foam passes away; what is of use to mankind remains in the earth.
the verse says what is of use to mankind remains, not only to one group
"as for that which is of use to mankind, it remaineth in the earth."
only official help, like a signed reference, really counts as benefit
in the parable, usefulness itself remains, whatever form it takes.

games.q: a new coworker at your part-time job keeps messing up the register. everyone's annoyed; nobody's helping. what fits today?
o: show them the one trick that took you weeks to figure out.
report it to the manager so the problem gets handled properly.
leave it; people learn best when they figure it out alone.
games.why: the annoyance is foam. what's useful stays. a small benefit, given person to person, is the water in the parable.

practice: Think of one person who could use something small from you: a ride, a read-through, an introduction, an honest word about work they're proud of.
During the sit, do the first piece of it: write the message, open the document, or set the reminder. One useful thing, done quietly.

wordCard.voice: An-Nafi'. The Benefactor, source of every benefit, named beside Ad-Darr, so that harm and help are known to be in one hand.

orig.note: Arabic: the Benefactor, from the traditional list of the Names; said together with Ad-Darr.

carryVoice: The line for today: benefit, the kind that stays like water after the foam is gone. Until tomorrow.

sources.q: as for that which is of use to mankind, it remaineth in the earth.

sources.ref: at-Tabarani, al-Mu'jam al-Awsat (the most beloved to God are the most useful to people)
Sahih Muslim 1009 (removing harm from the road is charity)
